description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of six from Vietnam, bringing together three members with backgrounds in economics and business and three experienced technology enthusiasts.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we have chosen the Space Mission Design Game challenge. We are particularly interested in how resource allocation, risk management, and engineering constraints influence real-world decisions.
summary:
IS-SPACE is a browser-based game for exploring the choices behind a space mission. Players assemble a spacecraft, check its mass, power, budget and estimated delta-v, then enter a 3D space scene. Exploration activities include viewing celestial bodies, answering astronomy questions and selecting samples in an illustrative landing scene.
The project addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by making engineering constraints visible while the player makes decisions. Adding an instrument can increase scientific capability, but it also adds mass, cost and power demand. We want players to notice those connections and explain their choices.
We developed the prototype in TypeScript and Three.js, building on the open-source WebGL-Orbiter project. The simulation uses simplified physics and game parameters. It is intended for introductory learning.
details:
IS-SPACE lets players explore how a spacecraft design changes when its equipment changes. The mission designer offers spacecraft, power sources, instruments, engines and launch vehicles. A set of checks shows whether a design meets the game's budget, mass, power and delta-v requirements before launch.

The 3D scene gives players a way to observe spacecraft motion and try attitude and thrust controls. The design panel uses the ideal rocket equation to estimate delta-v. Solar power calculations use a distance-based inverse-square relationship. These are teaching models: the flight simulation uses simplified gravity, and the equipment catalog includes both real-world references and fictional concepts. We do not present its prices or equipment parameters as flight-qualified specifications.

The latest version adds two exploration activities. In the first, players view a celestial body, open a reconnaissance scene and answer a short astronomy question. In the second, they select samples through a landing interface. The activities connect the mission setting with information about planets and materials. Their interface completion checks still need to be aligned with the separate mission-rule layer, so we treat this version as a prototype rather than a finished assessment tool.

We used TypeScript, Three.js, HTML, CSS and Webpack. GitHub holds the source and Netlify hosts the web application. The project builds on WebGL-Orbiter by Masahiro Sakuta. Our additions include the mission-design experience, exploration interactions, mission rules, report handling, save-data checks and a history interface. Server-side history components have been prepared, but authenticated, persistent cloud history is not yet complete.

Our educational goal is to help learners explain a decision rather than simply reach a score. For example, a player can compare two designs and discuss why carrying more equipment reduces the estimated delta-v when the propellant supply stays fixed. We have not yet measured learning gains in a classroom study.

We considered browser performance, readable controls, multilingual content and the distinction between scientific references and game assumptions. The next work is to bring the interface and mission rules into agreement, test the full experience with learners and complete reliable online storage.
